## Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Explain how Git tracks changes (commits, branches, merges) and resolve a
  merge conflict.
- Create and manage repositories on GitHub, and contribute through issues
  and pull requests.
- Authenticate to GitHub with SSH and **sign your commits**, so your work
  is verifiably yours.
- Collaborate in a team with a branch-based workflow — the one you will
  use for every practical work.
- Write documentation in **Markdown** — every README, report and
  specification you hand in this semester.

## Git

> Git is a free and open source distributed version control system (VCS)
> designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with
> speed and efficiency. — <https://git-scm.com/>

Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel source code,
Git tracks changes in a set of files and coordinates the work of several
people on the same code base. It is *the* version control system today —
you will use it in every course and every job from now on.

### Repositories and clones

A Git **repository** holds your project and its entire history. Git is
**distributed**: every **clone** is a full copy of the repository, history
included — you can work (and commit) offline, and synchronize later. By
convention the copy on GitHub is called the **remote** (`origin`), and the
copy on your machine is your local repository.

### Commits, hashes and tags

Git records changes as **commits** — snapshots of the project at a point
in time. Each commit has a unique **hash** computed from its content: a
commit cannot be modified without changing its hash, which is what makes
the history trustworthy.

- A **tag** is a human-friendly name for one commit — typically a release
  (`v1.0.0`).
- A commit can be **signed** to prove who authored it. You will set this
  up in the exercises: your commits will carry a "Verified" badge on
  GitHub.

### The three areas

Between your editor and the history sit three places:

1. The **working directory** — the files you edit.
2. The **staging area** — the changes you have marked for the next commit
   (`git add`).
3. The **repository** — the committed history (`git commit`).

`git status` shows where every change currently is; `git diff` shows what
changed but is not staged yet.

### Branches

A **branch** is a movable pointer to a commit — the default branch is
usually called `main`. Creating a branch is instantaneous (it is just a
pointer), which is why the standard way to develop a feature is: branch
off `main`, commit on the branch, merge back when ready. `HEAD` is the
pointer to wherever you currently are.

### Merging

Bringing a branch's work back is done in one of three ways:

- **Merge** — combine both branches in a new *merge commit* (the
  default).
- **Rebase** — replay your commits on top of the target branch, keeping a
  linear history.
- **Squash** — collapse the branch's commits into a single one before
  merging.

### Conflicts

When two people change the **same lines** of the same file, Git cannot
decide for you: the merge stops with a **conflict**, and marks the file:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
Here's a line added by you.
=======
Here's a line added by someone else.
>>>>>>> other-branch
```

You resolve it by editing the file (keep what should stay, delete the
markers), then `git add` the file and conclude the merge. You will
practice this in the exercises — deliberately.

### Ignoring files

A `.gitignore` file at the root of the repository lists what Git must not
track — build outputs, IDE configuration, secrets. Ignore by name,
extension or pattern:

```gitignore
# Ignore all text files...
*.txt

# ...except the input files of the examples
!examples/**/*_input.txt

# Ignore the target directory at the root only
/target/
```

Good practice: commit **source files only** — never build artifacts (like
Maven's `target/`) or binaries. Add entries as the need appears rather
than pasting a giant generated list.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Git cheat sheet"}
```sh
git clone <url>            # clone a repository
git status                 # what changed, and where it is
git diff [<file>]          # unstaged changes
git add <file>             # stage changes
git commit -m "Message"    # commit staged changes
git checkout -b <branch>   # create a branch and switch to it
git checkout <branch>      # switch branches
git merge <branch>         # merge a branch into the current one
git push                   # send your commits to the remote
git pull                   # fetch + integrate remote commits
git fetch                  # fetch remote state without touching files
git log                    # history (q to quit)
git tag <name>             # tag the current commit
```
:::

## GitHub

> GitHub is a platform and cloud-based service for software development
> and version control using Git. — <https://github.com>

GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration on top: issues, pull
requests, code review, discussions. It is also a social platform — your
profile and public repositories are a portfolio that recruiters actually
look at.

### Users and organizations

A repository belongs to a **user** or to an **organization** (shared by
members — this course lives in one, and each of your PW teams can create
one).

### Issues, pull requests and forks

- **Issues** track bugs, tasks and ideas; they can be assigned, labeled
  and discussed.
- A **pull request (PR)** proposes changes from a branch: teammates
  review, comment, request changes, approve — then the branch is merged.
- A **fork** is your own copy of someone else's repository — how you
  contribute to projects where you have no write access.

The standard contribution cycle:

1. Open an issue describing the change (optional but recommended — it
   avoids duplicated or unwanted work).
2. Create a branch (GitHub can create one directly from the issue).
3. Commit and push your changes on the branch.
4. Open a pull request; a teammate reviews it.
5. Merge, then delete the branch.

::: {.callout-tip}
As a HEIG-VD student you get GitHub Pro for free through
[GitHub Education](https://docs.github.com/en/education/explore-the-benefits-of-teaching-and-learning-with-github-education/github-global-campus-for-students).
:::

## Working in a team

For the practical works, your whole group has write access to one shared
repository. Two workflows exist; **we recommend the first**.

### Pull-request workflow (recommended)

Exactly the contribution cycle above, applied inside your team: one
branch per feature, one PR per branch, **a teammate (not the author)
reviews and merges**. The history stays readable and everyone sees what
enters `main`.

### Centralized workflow, and the rejected push

Some teams commit directly to `main`. Even then — and also on the PR
workflow whenever two branches touch `main` between your pull and your
push — you will eventually see this:

```text
> git push
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/...'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally.
```

Nothing is broken: a teammate pushed to `main` before you. The recovery
sequence:

```sh
# Once, the first time: replay your commits on top of theirs when pulling
git config --global pull.rebase true

# Integrate their work, then push yours
git pull
git push
```

If your changes and theirs touch the same lines, the pull stops with a
conflict: resolve the marked files (see [Conflicts](#conflicts)), then

```sh
git add <resolved-file>
git rebase --continue
git push
```

::: {.callout-important}
Practice this **before** the first practical work deadline — the rejected
push always shows up at the worst moment otherwise.
:::

## Markdown {#sec-markdown}

Code is only half of what you hand in. The other half — README files,
protocol specifications, practical-work reports — is written in
**Markdown**: plain text that stays readable as-is, but renders as
formatted text wherever it lands.

Created by John Gruber in 2004, it is now the default documentation
format of the industry: GitHub and GitLab render it, static site
generators build websites from it, and Pandoc converts it to PDF, HTML or
DOCX. Both this page and the slides that go with it are Markdown.

Two properties make it worth ten minutes of your time. It is **diffable**
— because it is plain text, Git shows you exactly which sentence changed,
which a `.docx` cannot. And it is **portable** — the same file is a
readable text file, a GitHub page and a PDF.

### Syntax

The whole language fits on one screen:

```markdown
# Heading 1
## Heading 2

**bold**, _italic_, ~~strikethrough~~, `inline code`

- bullet item
- another item

1. numbered item
2. another item

> A quote.

[link text](https://heig-vd.ch)
![alt text, for screen readers](./images/diagram.png)

| Column | Column |
| ------ | -----: |
| cell   |    123 |

---
```

Fenced code blocks are three backticks, with the language for syntax
highlighting — always name it, it is what makes a README readable:

````markdown
```java
System.out.println("Hello World!");
```
````

Two rules that catch everyone out: a **blank line separates blocks** (a
list glued to the paragraph above it will not render as a list), and a
**line break inside a paragraph is ignored** — wrap your source at 80
characters and it still renders as one paragraph.

When Markdown genuinely cannot express something, you can drop raw HTML
into the file. Use it sparingly; the point of Markdown is that the source
stays readable.

### Which Markdown?

Markdown was never standardised as one language, so implementations
differ slightly. Two matter to you:

- [CommonMark](https://commonmark.org/) — the strict, unambiguous
  specification most tools now follow.
- [GitHub Flavored Markdown](https://github.github.com/gfm/) (GFM) —
  CommonMark plus tables, task lists (`- [ ]`), strikethrough and
  autolinks. This is what GitHub renders, so this is what you write for
  READMEs and issues.

The [Markdown Guide](https://www.markdownguide.org/) is the reference to
keep open until the syntax is in your fingers.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — Configure your identity {#sec-ex1}

Your GitHub account and Git itself were installed in
[chapter 00](00-environment-setup.qmd). Finish the configuration:

1. [Verify your email address](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/signing-up-for-github/verifying-your-email-address)
   on GitHub if not done yet, and enable
   [two-factor authentication](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa)
   (strongly recommended).
2. Make sure Git knows you, **with the same email as your GitHub
   account**:

```sh
git config --global user.name "First-name Last-name"
git config --global user.email "your@email"
```

**Verification**: `git config --list` shows both values.

### Exercise 2 — SSH authentication {#sec-ex2}

SSH lets you push and pull without typing credentials — and it is the
authentication you will use all semester (you will learn how SSH itself
works in a later chapter).

1. [Generate an SSH key and add it to the ssh-agent](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent)
   — follow the **Linux** instructions on WSL, macOS instructions on
   macOS.
2. [Add the **public** key to your GitHub account](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/adding-a-new-ssh-key-to-your-github-account)
   as an **authentication key**.

::: {.callout-caution}
The **private** key never leaves your machine — treat it like a password,
and keep a backup of the key pair somewhere safe. The **public** key is
the only one you share.
:::

**Verification**: `ssh -T git@github.com` greets you by username.

### Exercise 3 — Sign your commits {#sec-ex3}

Signing proves a commit is really yours — signed commits get the
**Verified** badge on GitHub, and verifiable authorship matters when your
group's work is graded.

1. Add the **same public key** to GitHub once more, this time as a
   **signing key**.
2. Tell Git to sign every commit with it:

```sh
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgSign true
```

::: {.callout-warning}
SSH commit signing requires **Git 2.34 or newer** — check with
`git --version`. Any recent Ubuntu or Homebrew Git is fine; an old
preinstalled Git fails with cryptic errors.
:::

**Verification**: `git config --list` shows `gpg.format=ssh`,
`user.signingkey=...` and `commit.gpgsign=true`.

### Exercise 4 — Your profile README {#sec-ex4}

Time to use all of it. GitHub shows the `README.md` of a repository named
like your username as your **profile page** — your first repository will
be your own introduction to the world.

1. [Create the profile repository](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-github-profile/customizing-your-profile/managing-your-profile-readme)
   on GitHub (initialized with a README).
2. Clone it **with SSH** (repository page → **Code** → **SSH** tab):

```sh
git clone git@github.com:<username>/<username>.git
cd <username>
git log            # one commit, made by GitHub for you
```

3. Edit `README.md` — present yourself in
   [Markdown](#sec-markdown), and be creative. Use at least a heading, a
   list, a link, an image and one fenced code block, so you have written
   each construct once.
4. Walk the full cycle, watching each step:

```sh
git status         # README.md modified
git diff           # your changes, line by line
git add README.md
git status         # now staged
git commit -m "Update profile README"
git log            # your signed commit is HEAD, ahead of origin/main
git push
```

**Verification**: your profile shows the README, and the commit carries
the **Verified** badge on GitHub. If it does not, revisit
[exercise 3](#sec-ex3).

### Exercise 5 — Cause (and fix) a conflict {#sec-ex5}

In your profile repository, create a conflict on purpose:

1. `git checkout -b conflict-drill`, change a line of `README.md`,
   commit.
2. `git checkout main`, change **the same line** differently, commit.
3. `git merge conflict-drill` → conflict. Open the file, resolve the
   markers, `git add README.md`, `git commit`.

**Verification**: `git log` shows the merge commit; the file contains
what you decided — and no `<<<<<<<` markers.

### Exercise 6 — Your first pull request {#sec-ex6}

The practical works require the pull-request workflow — walk the full
cycle once, on your profile repository:

1. Create a branch and improve something in your README:

```sh
git checkout -b improve-readme
# edit README.md
git add README.md && git commit -m "Improve README"
git push -u origin improve-readme
```

2. On GitHub, open the **pull request** the banner offers you; read the
   diff as a reviewer would.
3. **Merge** the pull request, delete the branch, then locally:

```sh
git checkout main
git pull
git branch -d improve-readme
```

**Verification**: the merged PR appears in the repository's
**Pull requests → Closed** tab, and `git log` shows the merge.

::: {.callout-tip}
Not ready for review? Open a **draft** pull request. And in your team
repositories, enable *automatically delete head branches* in the
settings — merged branches clean themselves up.
:::

### Share your profile

Post the link to your profile in the course
[GitHub Discussions]({{< var discussions-url >}}) (category *Show and
tell*) — it tells us you completed the chapter, and everyone gets to meet
you.

## Test your knowledge

- What is the difference between the staging area and a commit?
- What is a branch, physically?
- Merge, rebase, squash: when would you use which?
- Why does a rejected push happen, and what is the fix?
- What does the Verified badge prove — and what does it *not* prove?
- Why is Markdown a better fit than a Word document for a file that lives
  in a Git repository?

## Go further {#sec-go-further}

Optional content — useful general knowledge, not required for the
evaluations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Markdown beyond READMEs"}
The same source can become a website, a slide deck or a PDF:
[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) (this site),
[Hugo](https://gohugo.io/) and [MkDocs](https://www.mkdocs.org/) for
sites, [Marp](https://marp.app/) for slides,
[Pandoc](https://pandoc.org/) for anything to anything. Each adds its own
extensions on top of CommonMark — check the tool's documentation before
assuming a construct works.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Commit message practice"}
No universal convention exists; being consistent matters most. A good
default: an infinitive verb plus a short description ("Add profile
README", "Fix port parsing"). Your team should pick one style in PW1 and
stick to it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Learn Git visually"}
- [Learn Git Branching](https://learngitbranching.js.org/) — interactive
  exercises, excellent for branches/merges/rebases.
- [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book) — the free reference book (the
  first ~125 pages cover everything in this chapter).
- [Atlassian Git tutorials](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/what-is-version-control) —
  from beginner to advanced.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Alternatives"}
Version control: Subversion, Mercurial. Forges:
[GitLab](https://gitlab.com/), [Gitea](https://gitea.io/),
[Codeberg](https://codeberg.org). Markup: AsciiDoc,
[Typst](https://typst.app/), LaTeX (consider it for your thesis).
:::
